```{r}
#| warning: false
# Load packages
library(survival)
library(ggsurvfit)

# Set seed
set.seed(10)

# Sample size
n <- 1e3

# Parameters
a <- 2
sigma <- sqrt(2)
p_censor <- 0.2
n_censor <- round(p_censor * n)

# Generate data
t <- rweibull(n = n,
              shape = a,
              scale = sigma)
t <- sort(t)
status <- rep(x = 1,
              times = n)

# Censoring times
censor_times <- rbeta(n = n_censor,
                      shape1 = 1,
                      shape2 = 5) * max(t) * 0.6
censor_times <- sort(censor_times)

# Create three additional data sets
# This code relies on t and censor_times being sorted from low to high
t_ind <- t_low <- t_hig <- t
status_ind <- status_low <- status_hig <- status
for(i in 1:n_censor){
  # Independent
  indices_ind <- which(t_ind >= censor_times[i])
  censor_this <- sample(x = indices_ind,
                        size = 1)
  t_ind[censor_this] <- censor_times[i]
  status_ind[censor_this] <- 0
  
  # Low
  indices_low <- which(t_low >= censor_times[i])
  censor_this <- min(indices_low)
  t_low[censor_this] <- censor_times[i]
  status_low[censor_this] <- 0
  
  # High
  indices_hig <- which(t_hig >= censor_times[i])
  censor_this <- max(indices_hig)
  t_hig[censor_this] <- censor_times[i]
  status_hig[censor_this] <- 0
}



### Kaplan-Meier curves
# Plot names
# sample(x = LETTERS[1:4],
#        size = 4)

# No censoring
ggsurvfit(survfit2(Surv(time = t,
                        event = status) ~ 1)) +
  labs(x = "Years",
       y = "Probability of Survival",
       title = "Plot D") +
  add_risktable()


# Independent censoring
ggsurvfit(survfit2(Surv(time = t_ind,
                        event = status_ind) ~ 1)) +
  labs(x = "Years",
       y = "Probability of Survival",
       title = "Plot A") +
  add_risktable()


# Low censoring
ggsurvfit(survfit2(Surv(time = t_low,
                        event = status_low) ~ 1)) +
  labs(x = "Years",
       y = "Probability of Survival",
       title = "Plot C") +
  add_risktable()


# High censoring
ggsurvfit(survfit2(Surv(time = t_hig,
                        event = status_hig) ~ 1)) +
  labs(x = "Years",
       y = "Probability of Survival",
       title = "Plot B") +
  add_risktable()

```


Each of the four Kaplan-Meier curves above was created using the same 1,000 survival times.
Three of the plots have censoring; one does not.
The censoring times are identical in the three plots that have censoring.
In one of the plots, censoring is independent of survival time.
In another plot, censoring is an indication that the event will occur soon.
In another plot, censoring is an indication that the event
will not occur for a long time.

Each plot has a risk table below it,
displaying the number of people at risk at time $t$
and the number of events that have occurred by time $t$.

## Problem 1

(4 points)
In each plot, what is the probability of surviving
past one year?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

Plot A: Between 0.5625 and 0.625

Plot B: Between 0.5 and 0.5625

Plot C: About 0.75

Plot D: Between 0.5625 and 0.625

:::

## Problem 2

(4 points)
In each plot, what is the probability of an event occurring
in the first two years?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

Plot A: Approximately 0.875

Plot B: 1

Plot C: Approximately 0.8

Plot D: Approximately 0.875

:::

## Problem 3

(1 point)
How many people were censored between 1 and 2 years?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

Consider Plot A.
The number of people at risk dropped from 469 to 102,
meaning $469-102 = 367$ people either had an event or were censored.
The number of events was $698 - 340 = 358$.
So, $367 - 358 = 9$ people were censored.

:::



## Problem 4

(1 point)
In Plot C, how many observed events occurred between 0 and 6 months?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

Zero. The curve only drops when there's an event,
and the curve is flat over this range of times.

:::
    
## Problem 5

(1 point)
Which plot has no censoring?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

Plot D.
We know this is true because Plot D has the most events
by Year 3.

:::

## Problem 6

(1 point)
In which plot is censoring an indication that the event
will not occur for a long time?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

Plot B.
Recall that censoring times are identical in the three plots
that have censoring.
If censoring is an indication that the event will not occur
for a long time,
then censoring will eliminate later event times.
Plot B has no events after about two years.
So, it must be Plot B that has censoring long before the actual
event time.

:::

## Problem 7

(1 point)
In which plot is censoring an indication that the event will
occur soon?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

Plot C.
Recall that censoring times are identical in the three plots
that have censoring.
If censoring is an indication that the event will occur soon,
then censoring will eliminate earlier event times.
Plot C has no events between 0 and six months.
So, it must be Plot C that has censoring just before the actual
event time.

Another way to reason through this:
Note that Plot C and Plot D have the same number of people at risk
at each year.
Plot C has censoring, but Plot D does not.
This means that in Plot C, the censoring times were almost at the same time as the
actual event times.

:::

## Problem 8

(1 point)
In which plot is censoring independent of survival time?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

Plot A.
This plot has the most similar curve to Plot D,
but with fewer events by year 3.

:::

## Problem 9

(4 points)
For each plot, state whether the last observed time was an event time
or a censoring time.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

For each plot, the last observed time was an event time.

In each plot, the survival curve hits zero.
If the last observed time was a censoring time,
the survival curve would have to be positive at its right-most point.

:::
